strengths: Simple, training-free, inference-only planner (DUS) that is a genuine drop-in replacement for confidence-based unmasking in semi-AR masked diffusion decoding, requiring no architectural or training changes.

Broad empirical evaluation: five masked diffusion LLMs (LLaDA-Base/Instruct, Dream-Instruct, DiffuCoder-Base/Instruct) across six benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, BBH, MMLU-Pro), with consistent improvements over the self-confidence baseline at matched NFE budgets, with large gains at aggressive speedups (e.g., GSM8K LLaDA-Instruct 18.73 vs 57.09 at B=64).

Informative ablation (Table 3) that disentangles the planner signal from the dilation schedule itself: random unmasking + dilated-incremental scheduling dramatically outperforms random + fixed-k, providing empirical support for the core hypothesis that spacing unmasked tokens reduces mutual information and approximation error.
Additional analysis (Appendix A.2) showing larger block sizes with DUS can improve accuracy under a fixed total NFE budget, which is a useful practical finding.

Reasonable related-work coverage situating DUS against self-planners, learned planners (P2), semi-AR block diffusion, entropy-bounded unmasking, and KV-cache methods; evaluation protocol details (few-shot settings, sample counts, early stopping) are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical 'guarantees' are overstated. Lemma 1 is an approximation ('≈'), not a bound, and rests on the assumption that text is a stationary, ergodic, fast-mixing first-order Markov chain — an assumption plainly violated by natural language and by the autoregressive conditioning structure of the denoiser. No empirical validation of ρ or correlation decay at the distances used by the dilation pattern is provided, so the claimed proximity to the joint-entropy bound is unverified. The proof of Lemma 1 is also loose: transition (a) invokes a first-order Markov property to drop conditioning, the per-pair ε bound requires all chosen pairs separated by distance D (which depends on k and is never checked), and no argument is given that the dilation pattern is optimal among schedules — the paper claims DUS 'minimizes' entropy without proving any optimality.

Missing comparison to the strongest related baselines. EB-Sampler (Ben-Hamu et al. 2025) is described as achieving 2–3× speedups with an entropy-bounded scheme, and entropy/margin planners are discussed, but the empirical comparison is restricted to a single self-confidence baseline with fixed k = log2 B. Without these comparisons it is hard to judge whether DUS actually advances the speed–quality frontier or merely improves one particular planner.

Evaluation metrics conflate planner quality with block-size effects. Speedup is defined via NFE (B/log2 B) rather than wall-clock latency; since each denoiser pass still processes the full sequence, the practical speedup at, e.g., B=64 may differ substantially. Additionally, both planners are forced to the same B, and the paper's own results (DiffuCoder-Instruct on HumanEval, where DUS scores drop from 22.56 to 8.54 at higher speeds; non-monotone code results) contradict the blanket claims that DUS 'consistently improves' and achieves gains 'across all datasets and speedups'.

Statistical rigor is thin: no confidence intervals, seeds, or variance estimates; HumanEval has only 164 samples and ablations use only 300 GSM8K samples, so many reported differences (especially in Table 2, where gains are 1–5 points on ~540 samples) are within plausible noise. The skip-mechanism component mentioned in Section 3 is never evaluated.

Presentation and polish issues: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('instroduced', 'knoeledge', 'model-free agnostic planner', inconsistent verb agreement), a Table 2 caption listing block sizes {8,16,32,64} while only {16,32} are reported, a partially garbled abstract sentence, and notation in Eq. (6)–(7) that is difficult to parse. These errors reduce confidence in overall carefulness.
No code release is stated, and reproducibility relies on reproducing a nonstandard MATH500 task class and custom BBH/MMLU-Pro subsampling from the appendix description alone.

strengths: The core idea is simple and practical: a deterministic, inference-only dilated unmasking schedule that requires no retraining or auxiliary planner, making it a genuine drop-in technique for existing MDLMs.

Empirical coverage is broad: four block sizes (B = 8, 16, 32, 64) across six benchmarks and five models (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder base and instruct variants), with DUS consistently beating the self-confidence planner at matched NFE budgets in most cells of Tables 1-2.

The ablation in Table 3 (fixed-k vs. dilated-incremental schedules crossed with confidence and random planners) is informative and supports the mechanism the authors propose: dilated spacing helps most when the planner itself is uninformative, and the block-size experiment in Appendix A.2 adds a useful additional data point.

The paper is candid that the quality degrades as speedup increases and shows the full speed-quality frontier rather than only cherry-picked operating points, and Figures 1b/1c give a nice qualitative illustration of premature chain-of-thought truncation.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weak and rests on assumptions that do not hold for text. Lemma 1 requires the sequence to be a fast-mixing, first-order Markov chain and concludes only an approximation (≈), not a guarantee. Language is neither first-order Markov nor demonstrably fast-mixing, and the paper provides no evidence (e.g., measured maximal correlation or MI decay) that the assumptions are even approximately satisfied. Moreover, Lemma 1 is close to tautological: it says that nearly independent variables have nearly additive joint entropy, which does not establish that the specific dilation pattern is optimal, contrary to the framing in Section 3.6.

The proof of Lemma 1 has gaps: transition (a) replaces conditional MI with the full previous set by MI with only the immediately preceding selected token, which does not follow from first-order Markov on the underlying chain when intermediate positions are still masked; transition (b) applies the pairwise bound to what are O(k^2) pairs but only budgets epsilon per pair; and H(X_{i1}) in (12) is missing conditioning on S_t. As written, the 'theoretical guarantee' claimed in the contributions list is not established.

Baselines are too limited. The only comparison at matched budgets is against the self-confidence planner with fixed k. Cited competitors such as EB-Sampler (Ben-Hamu et al. 2025), P2, entropy/margin planners, and existing remasking schedules are not evaluated, so it is impossible to know whether DUS advances the state of the art or merely beats one heuristic. There is also no comparison against alternative deterministic spread-out patterns (e.g., random spread, interleaved offsets), which is essential to attribute gains to the specific dilation design rather than to spacing alone.
No wall-clock latency measurements. All speedup claims are derived from an NFE accounting formula (Eq. 13); actual end-to-end latency, which practitioners care about, is never reported.

Statistical rigor is lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests anywhere, despite evaluating on small datasets (HumanEval has 164 samples; Table 3 uses only 300 GSM8K samples). Several results show large variance (e.g., DiffuCoder-Base jumping from 6.71 to 38.41 Pass@1 between planners at B=16), which the paper attributes to 'already low performance' without further analysis. Some cells are anomalous (e.g., DiffuCoder-Instruct at B=32 HumanEval where DUS underperforms the baseline), undermining the 'consistently outperforms' claim.

The 'Skip Mechanism' is presented as one of three core features of DUS, but it is never evaluated, ablated, or assigned hyperparameters (threshold value is unspecified), so the method actually tested is underspecified relative to the method described.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: numerous grammatical errors ('instroduced', 'knoeledge', 'unmasked them in parallel', 'a inference-only'), a broken reference URL ('urlhttps://...'), an inconsistent Table 2 caption (claims B = {8,16,32,64} but reports {16,32}), and a confusing sentence in Related Work stating that semi-AR block diffusion 'does not reduce the total number of denoiser passes from O(G) to O(G/B)' which contradicts the surrounding argument.

The entropy-based justification is muddled. Equation (5) is used to argue that confidence-based planners incur 'higher entropy gain', but the direction of the argument is unclear: unmasking low-confidence (high-entropy) tokens, as DUS's spacing-first schedule effectively does early on, increases immediate entropy consumed. The link between 'minimizing joint conditional entropy gain' and generation quality (accuracy, pass@1) is asserted rather than demonstrated, and no metric of generation quality beyond benchmark scores (e.g., perplexity of reasoning traces) is provided.

No code release is mentioned, and reproducibility details are incomplete (e.g., sampling temperature, remasking specifics per model, the exact procedure when |P_R| < |P_{R-1}|), making independent verification difficult.

strengths: Simple, inference-only, model-agnostic method (DUS) that requires no retraining and is a drop-in replacement for confidence-based planners in standard semi-AR MDLM decoding.

Consistent empirical gains across multiple model families (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, DiffuCoder-7B) and diverse benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, BBH, MMLU-Pro) at matched NFE budgets, with large improvements at aggressive speedups (e.g., GSM8K 38.7 vs 65.7 at 6.4x).

The ablation in Table 3 is informative and well-designed: it isolates the dilated-incremental schedule from planner guidance, showing that even a random planner recovers most accuracy under dilation, which supports the core hypothesis about reducing mutual information between simultaneously unmasked tokens.
The appendix block-size experiment (Table 5) is a useful additional lever analysis, showing quality gains under a fixed total NFE budget by trading block size against iterations.
The paper is transparent about evaluation protocols (NFE accounting, early stopping, few-shot COT settings, dataset subsets) in Appendix A.1.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is much weaker than advertised. Lemma 1 is only an approximation result ('≈') relying on strong assumptions (stationary, ergodic, fast-mixing first-order Markov chain) that plainly do not hold for natural language; the proof of Eq. (12) via transition (b) drops pairwise MI terms beyond adjacent indices, and the choice of separation D satisfying I < eps/(k-1) is circular for large k/B since D may exceed the block size. The paper claims DUS 'minimizes' entropy gain and has 'theoretical guarantees,' but no comparison against baselines' entropy is actually proven.

Baseline coverage is thin: the only comparison is the self-confidence planner at matched NFE. Adaptive/entropy-based methods the paper itself discusses, notably EB-Sampler (Ben-Hamu et al. 2025) and P2 (Peng et al. 2025), are not evaluated, making it hard to establish that DUS is actually the strongest planner at these budgets.

No wall-clock latency or throughput measurements. All 'speedups' are NFE ratios; while these should correlate with FLOPs, actual end-to-end speedups (especially on V100s, without KV caching) are not reported, which matters for a paper whose central claim is acceleration.

Several unexplained or unexplored findings: base models beating instruct models on code under DUS (Section 4.2), non-monotonic code results at high speedup, and the Skip Mechanism (Section 3.6, feature 3) is described but never ablated or used in experiments.
Statistical rigor is limited: no error bars or significance tests, ablations on only the first 300 GSM8K samples, and hand-picked subsets of BBH (20/subtask) and MMLU-Pro (40/subtask).

Presentation quality is below par: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('instroduced', 'knoeledge', 'compares multiple planner strategies', 'chose'), broken reference URLs ('urlhttps://...'), inconsistent notation between Eq. (6)-(7) and the example, and missing code release, which hurts reproducibility.
The framing that DUS 'reveals the true speed-quality frontier of MDLMs' is overclaimed given the restricted baseline set and NFE-only speed measurement.

strengths: DUS is a simple, deterministic, model-agnostic inference-time planner that turns the MDLM quality-speed trade-off into a predictable knob (block size B), a genuinely useful property for practitioners; the 5.8× wall-clock speedup claim is substantiated by an end-to-end timing benchmark (Table 12), not just NFE accounting.

The entropy-gap framing (Lemma 3.3, Corollary 3.4) gives a clean conceptual account of why confidence-based parallel unmasking fails: per-token planners minimize a marginal surrogate that is loose when co-decoded indices are coupled. The token-distance analysis (Table 11, Figure 4) provides direct empirical evidence that DUS achieves 2-3× wider spacing and 100% isolated co-decoded tokens, connecting mechanism to outcome.

Extensive empirical validation: 5 MDLM variants across 7 benchmarks (math, code, general knowledge, instruction following), with ablations covering block size, skip threshold, dilation base, level skip, single-block (B=G) regime, per-step runtime breakdown, and head-to-head comparisons with EB/CB adaptive samplers (B.9).

The matched-parallelism ablation (Table 3) is well designed: it isolates that the benefit comes from spacing-aware scheduling rather than merely revealing more tokens per step, including a random-planner control that shows dilated-incremental schedules recover much of the fixed-k loss.

The hybrid extension (dilated spacing as a post-filter for EB/CB samplers, Table 4/Figure 6) demonstrates that the core spacing principle generalizes beyond the specific DUS schedule, strengthening the contribution beyond a single method.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly states the VLMC fast-mixing assumption is 'an analytical device... not a literal claim about all data,' acknowledges failure modes (aggressive parallelism on globally constrained tasks), and discloses LLM usage and hardware/protocol details that support reproducibility (public code, lm-eval-harness).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are weakly connected to the method's actual performance. The D_ε threshold in Lemma 3.5 is never quantified or estimated for any real model or dataset, and the fast-mixing VLMC assumption is far from language (natural text has strong long-range dependencies that the paper itself concedes). The theory therefore serves as motivation rather than a prediction that is tested; the paper's own fallback is purely empirical validation.

Statistical rigor is limited: no confidence intervals, standard errors, or significance tests are reported anywhere, despite some evaluations on small subsets (BBH: 540 samples, MMLU-Pro: 560, GSM8K ablations: 300 samples, wall-clock: 105 samples). Several claimed gains (e.g., BBH +1-5%) could be within sampling noise.

Head-to-head positioning against adaptive samplers is ambiguous. Figure 5/Table 12 show DUS sits at the lowest-NFE end but with lower accuracy than EB/CB at matched settings (e.g., EB γ=1.0 reaches 71.72% GSM8K at 2.8× vs DUS 59.51% at 3.9×). The paper acknowledges this, but abstract-level claims like 'outperforms confidence-based planners' and 'improves adaptive samplers' could give a stronger impression than the Pareto evidence supports; DUS dominates only at aggressive speedups, not across the frontier.

Parameter sensitivity results are surprising and under-explained: Table 9 shows the alternative dilation bases a=3,4 collapse accuracy dramatically (e.g., 19.2→6.4 on MATH500), yet these cells also have very different NFE, so accuracy and cost are confounded and the reported comparisons are not at matched budgets. This fragility of the 'robust' defaults deserves a clearer analysis (is it step count, spacing pattern, or something else?).

The theoretical analysis conditions on Assumption 3.1 (optimal estimator), yet the paper later attributes DUS's advantage partly to denoiser miscalibration under the semi-AR masking distribution (Section 3.3). The interplay between the two effects—entropy gap under the true distribution vs. planner behavior under a miscalibrated denoiser—is not disentangled, leaving the causal story partially speculative.

Some experimental details reduce comparability: DiffuCoder baselines use a different protocol (semi-AR disabled), the self-confidence baseline fixes k=log2 B which may not be its strongest configuration, and confidence metrics differ across models (probability vs. entropy 'as in their original work'), which introduces confounds when reading Table 1.

strengths: The core contribution is practical and well-scoped: DUS is an inference-only, model-agnostic, deterministic planner that converts the quality-speed trade-off into a predictable operating point controlled by block size B, requiring no retraining or architectural changes.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for a scheduling paper: 5 MDLM variants across 7 benchmarks (math, code, knowledge, instruction following), with matched-NFE comparisons against self-confidence planners, and against adaptive EB/CB samplers (Appendix B.9, Figure 5).

The paper does not overstate the theory: it explicitly frames the VLMC fast-mixing assumption as an analytical device rather than a literal claim about language, and the entropy-gap framing (Lemma 3.3, Corollary 3.4) gives a clean and correct motivation for why spacing should help parallel unmasking.

The key ablation (Section 4.3, Table 3) isolates the effect of spreading from mere parallelism: with equal average k, dilated-incremental beats fixed-k, and the token-distance analysis (Table 11) empirically confirms the spacing mechanism (100% isolated co-decoded tokens, 2-3x wider pairwise distances).
Wall-clock results (Table 12) and per-step runtime breakdown (Table 10) show that sampler overhead is negligible and the NFE speedup translates to real latency gains (5.8x at B=32).

The hybrid extension (Section 4.4, Table 4, Figure 6) demonstrates that the spacing principle is composable as a post-filter on EB/CB samplers, with a broad (gamma, tau, g0) sweep supporting the claim.
weaknesses: Originality is modest: the idea of revealing spatially distributed tokens coarse-to-fine is an intuitive extension of semi-AR block diffusion, and the connection to cosine/non-uniform schedules and prior fixed-schedule work is acknowledged but not sharply differentiated. The novelty is more an empirical finding than a new mechanism.

The theoretical guarantees are weak in a quantitatively meaningful way: Lemma 3.5 only asserts existence of a distance threshold D_epsilon with no estimate of its magnitude, so there is no way to verify from the theory that the actual spacings s_t used by DUS (which shrink geometrically) yield small entropy gaps. The later-iteration regime, where most tokens are decoded and dependencies are strongest, is explicitly not covered by the theory.

The headline framing oversells quality retention. The claim of 'recovering most of the performance lost' holds only relative to the confidence planner at matched speedup; relative to token-by-token decoding, accuracy still drops substantially at the advertised operating points (e.g., GSM8K 72.63% -> 49.36% at the headline 5.8x speedup; Table 12 also shows EB/CB dominate DUS at reasonable accuracy levels). The 5.8x speedup claim and the accuracy claim are not achieved simultaneously.

Statistical rigor is thin: no confidence intervals, seeds, or variance estimates are reported anywhere. Several tables show gaps of 1-3 points on benchmarks with 150-560 subsampled examples (BBH, MMLU-Pro) or 164 HumanEval problems, and the paper itself notes that MBPP trends are 'less smooth,' which suggests some reported gains may not be statistically robust.

Reproducibility statement is incomplete: the abstract states 'Code is available at' with a missing URL, and Appendix A.3 ends with 'publicly available at for reproducibility' followed by nothing. This must be fixed.

The claimed orthogonality to KV-caching methods (Fast-dLLM, dKV-Cache) is asserted but never demonstrated empirically, even though these are the strongest competing acceleration approaches and the relevant question for practitioners is whether DUS stacks with them.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled: for DiffuCoder baselines semi-AR inference is disabled 'as in their original work' while DUS uses it, and the B=G single-block regime is relegated to the appendix where accuracy collapses (e.g., HumanEval at ~10-17%), weakening the 'up to 51x' narrative.

Presentation issues: Figure 1a axes/labels are hard to parse, Table 8/10 have unusual layouts, and some notation (S_t defined both as sampler state and as conditioning context S_1) is used loosely throughout the theory section.

strengths: The core contribution—a deterministic dilated unmasking schedule for block-wise MDLM decoding—is simple, inference-only, model-agnostic, and clearly useful: it turns the quality–speed trade-off into a predictable operating point set by B, with negligible planner overhead (Table 10) and verified wall-clock gains (5.8× over token-by-token, Table 12).

Empirical validation is unusually thorough: 5 models (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder), 6 benchmarks spanning math/code/knowledge/instruction-following, ablations over block size, dilation base, skip threshold, fixed-k vs. incremental-k schedules (Table 3), single-block B=G regime (Table 8), token-spacing analysis (Table 11), and runtime/wall-clock breakdowns.

The entropy-gap framing (Lemma 3.3, Corollary 3.4) gives a clean conceptual account of why per-token confidence planners fail under parallel unmasking, and the token-distance analysis (Table 11, Figure 4) empirically connects spacing to accuracy.

The hybrid extension (dilated spacing as a post-filter on EB/CB samplers, Section 4.4, Algorithm 1) demonstrates the spacing principle generalizes beyond the fixed schedule, with gains up to +13.4% in some settings.

The paper is largely honest about scope: it acknowledges the VLMC fast-mixing assumption is 'primarily an analytical device,' reports cases where EB/CB beat DUS at higher NFE, and states DUS should be viewed as a heuristic when long-range dependencies are strong.

Reproducibility support is reasonable: code release is promised, evaluation uses standard harnesses (lm-eval-harness), datasets/settings are precisely specified, and wall-clock/NFE accounting is transparent.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are weakly connected to the actual system. Assumption 3.1 (the denoiser equals the true conditional distribution) is far from reality, and the fast-mixing VLMC model of language is highly idealized. Moreover, Lemma 3.5 only asserts existence of a threshold D_ε; nothing quantifies whether DUS's actual spacings (s_1 = B/2, etc.) approach D_ε, and Lemma 3.6's constant C implicitly depends on M despite being stated as uniform. The theory motivates but does not predict the empirical behavior.

The headline claim of up to 5.8× speedup is accurate only in the NFE/wall-clock sense; absolute quality degrades steeply (e.g., Dream-Instruct HumanEval drops 57.9% → 14.6% already at 2.7×; LLaDA-B HumanEval 34.8% → 25.6% at 2.7×). 'Recovers most of the performance lost' is overstated in several operating regimes, and the practical use case (moderate B=16–32 with 40–50% relative accuracy retention) is narrower than the framing suggests.

Against the strongest baselines (EB/CB samplers), DUS occupies only the lowest-NFE corner of the accuracy–NFE frontier (Appendix B.9); at comparable NFE, adaptive samplers often dominate. The post-filter gains in Table 4 come with substantially higher NFE (e.g., HumanEval EB: 24.4/35 → 37.8/59, a 68% NFE increase), so 'matched or modestly higher NFE' should be stated more carefully.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing: the self-confidence planner uses fixed k = log2 B, and the ablation itself shows fixed-k slightly outperforms incremental-k for confidence-based planners (Table 3), so part of DUS's advantage over the confidence baseline may stem from schedule shape rather than spacing per se; a spaced confidence planner is absent.

Novelty is modest: dilation/spacing is a natural heuristic, and semi-AR block decoding with fewer iterations per block is well explored; the main insight is an empirical one (spatial spreading helps), which the paper attributes to an entropy-gap argument that only loosely formalizes it.

Some presentation issues: the code link in the abstract is left blank ('Code is available at'), MATH500 is described as 'cherry-picked' samples without discussion of implications, and several results (e.g., MBPP trends, occasional post-filter regressions on Dream CB) are explained only post hoc.
